title: Patient Assessment
summary: The one mental model you run on every patient, every call: size up the scene, hunt for life threats, decide sick or not sick, then build the story and recheck it.

lessons.title: The first 30 seconds: scene size-up
lessons.body:
## You cannot help anyone if you get hurt

Every call starts the same way. Before you touch a patient you answer a short list of questions about the place you are standing in. That list is the **scene size-up**, it runs in your head in seconds, and on the exam it is the first thing graded.

The order is not arbitrary. It moves outward from you, to the scene, to the patient, to the help you are going to need.

## The six questions

1. **Body substance isolation (BSI) and personal protective equipment (PPE).** Gloves on every single call. Add eye protection and a mask when blood, vomit, or coughing is likely, and a gown for childbirth or heavy bleeding. On the skill sheet you say it out loud, as in "BSI, gloves and eye protection", or you lose the point.
2. **Is the scene safe?** Traffic, fire, downed wires, unstable vehicles, chemicals, dogs, weapons, angry people. If it is not safe you do not enter. You stage at a safe distance and wait for police or fire.
3. **Mechanism of injury (MOI) or nature of illness (NOI)?** Trauma or medical. The bent steering column, the starred windshield, the height of a fall tell you what forces hit the body. For medical calls you ask the patient, the family, or the caller why 911 was dialed.
4. **How many patients?** Count before you commit to one. One crew handles one or two patients. Three or more turns the call into a multiple-casualty incident and changes everything about how you work.
5. **What else do I need?** More ambulances, an ALS (paramedic) intercept, fire for extrication, police for scene control, the utility company for wires. Request early. Help you cancel costs nothing, help you request late costs minutes you do not have.
6. **Do I need spinal precautions?** Decide from mechanism plus findings, not reflex. Current practice is to hold manual in-line stabilization of the head when the mechanism could have loaded the spine and the patient has midline neck or back pain, numbness or weakness, altered mental status, intoxication, or a distracting injury. An awake, sober, pain-free patient with a normal exam does not need a collar.

> **Trap:** Scene safe is not a box you tick once at the door. A quiet apartment turns loud when the boyfriend comes home. Re-check safety continuously and know where your exit is before you kneel down.

## Standard precautions are the floor, not the ceiling

"Standard precautions" means you treat every patient's blood and body fluid as infectious, because you cannot tell by looking. Gloves for all patient contact. Eye protection any time fluid can splash: suctioning, intubation assistance, childbirth, major bleeding, a coughing patient. An N95 respirator for suspected airborne disease such as tuberculosis or measles.

## What size-up buys you

By the time you reach the patient you already know whether this is trauma or medical, whether you have enough hands, whether more resources are coming, and whether you are holding the head. Everything after this is faster because of it.

> **On the exam:** The NREMT patient assessment skill sheet awards separate points for BSI, scene safety, MOI/NOI, number of patients, additional resources, and the spinal decision. They are six different points. Verbalize all six.
keyPoints: Size-up = BSI/PPE, scene safety, MOI vs NOI, number of patients, additional resources, spinal decision.
If the scene is unsafe you stage and wait; you do not become the second patient.
Call for extra resources early, because canceling is free and late requests cost minutes.
Spinal precautions come from mechanism plus findings, not from reflex.
Scene safety is reassessed continuously, not once at the door.

checks.q: You arrive at a two-car crash. Before stepping out of the ambulance, which of these is the first thing you should have addressed?
choices: Gloves and eye protection
The patient's chief complaint
A baseline set of vitals
SAMPLE history from the driver
checks.why: BSI/PPE comes before any patient contact. Complaint, vitals, and history all require you to already be at the patient's side.

checks.q: Dispatch sends you for one patient. On arrival there are four injured people. What is your immediate action?
choices: Begin treating the most obviously injured person
Request additional resources and start triage
Load the closest patient and leave
Complete a full assessment on each patient in turn
checks.why: Three or more patients exceeds one crew. You call for help and triage before you commit your hands to any single patient.

checks.q: Which patient most clearly needs manual in-line stabilization of the head?
choices: Sober adult, rear-ended at low speed, no pain, normal neuro exam
Adult who fell 15 feet and now reports midline neck pain
Adult with chest pain and no trauma history
Child with a fever and a sore throat
checks.why: A significant mechanism plus midline neck pain is the classic indication. A pain-free, sober patient with a normal exam and a minor mechanism does not need it, and neither medical patient has any spinal mechanism at all.

lessons.title: Primary survey: find it, fix it, keep going
lessons.body:
## The primary survey is a hunt, not an exam

The **primary survey** (also called the primary assessment) has exactly one job: find the things that will kill this patient in the next few minutes and fix them before you move on. It is not a head-to-toe exam. It takes 60 to 90 seconds.

One rule makes it work: **when you find a life threat, you stop and treat it right there.** You do not finish the checklist first. An open airway now beats a complete survey later.

## General impression, then level of consciousness

Before you touch anyone, look. From the doorway you form a **general impression**: rough age, how sick, what position, what color, how hard they are working to breathe. A patient sitting bolt upright, leaning on their hands (tripoding), gray, speaking in three-word sentences is half diagnosed from ten feet away.

Then level of consciousness with **AVPU**:

- **A, Alert.** Eyes open, engaging with you. Then test orientation to person, place, time, and event, which is charted as "alert and oriented times four".
- **V, Verbal.** Responds only when you speak loudly.
- **P, Painful.** Responds only to a trapezius pinch or sternal rub.
- **U, Unresponsive.** Nothing.

Anything below A is an airway problem waiting to happen, because the tongue falls back when muscle tone goes.

## XABCDE

The classic order is ABC. Trauma care put an **X** in front of it, because a patient can bleed out from one thigh in three minutes with a perfect airway.

- **X, exsanguinating hemorrhage.** Bright red spurting or a pool that is growing. Direct pressure first. If that fails, a commercial tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above the wound, tightened until the bleeding stops, with the time of application written on the tag.
- **A, airway.** Open and staying open? Snoring means the tongue. Gurgling means fluid and needs suction, no more than 10 seconds at a time in an adult. Open with a head-tilt chin-lift, or a jaw thrust if trauma is possible.
- **B, breathing.** Rate, depth, effort, symmetry. Look for accessory muscle use, retractions, unequal chest rise. An adult breathing slower than 8 or faster than 30 per minute with poor tidal volume gets bag-valve-mask ventilations at 1 breath every 6 seconds, which is 10 per minute.
- **C, circulation.** A palpable radial pulse means a systolic roughly 80 mmHg or better. Carotid only is a bad sign. Assess skin color, temperature, and moisture, plus capillary refill, where normal is under 2 seconds. Control any bleeding you have not already stopped.
- **D, disability.** Fast neuro check: AVPU again, pupils, and gross movement and sensation in all four limbs.
- **E, expose and environment.** Cut away what you need to see, look, then cover the patient with a blanket. Cold patients clot worse and bleed more, which is why hypothermia is one leg of the trauma death spiral.

> **Key:** The primary survey ends with one decision, not a diagnosis: is this patient a high priority for transport, yes or no.

> **On shift:** In the emergency department the same sequence runs at the door of the resuscitation bay. The trauma team calls it the primary survey too, and the tech who already has the patient exposed, on the monitor, and warm has done half of it.
keyPoints: Primary survey finds and fixes immediate life threats in 60 to 90 seconds; treat as you find.
General impression and AVPU come before you touch the patient.
XABCDE: exsanguinating bleeding, airway, breathing, circulation, disability, expose and environment.
Adults breathing under 8 or over 30 per minute with poor volume need BVM at 1 breath every 6 seconds.
A radial pulse suggests a systolic of about 80 mmHg or higher; carotid only is ominous.

checks.q: During the primary survey you hear gurgling on every breath. What do you do next?
choices: Finish the survey, then suction
Suction the airway for up to 10 seconds
Apply a nonrebreather at 15 L/min
Obtain a full set of vitals
checks.why: Gurgling is fluid in the airway and is a life threat. You treat it the moment you find it, and adult suctioning is limited to about 10 seconds at a time because you are also removing oxygen.

checks.q: An adult trauma patient has a spurting wound to the thigh and snoring respirations. Which do you address first?
choices: The snoring airway
The spurting thigh wound
Spinal stabilization
Exposure and warming
checks.why: The X in XABCDE comes before A precisely for this case. Massive external hemorrhage kills faster than a partially obstructed airway, and a tourniquet takes seconds.

checks.q: A patient opens her eyes and moans only when you pinch her trapezius. How do you score her on AVPU?
choices: Alert
Verbal
Painful
Unresponsive
checks.why: Response only to a painful stimulus is P. Verbal would mean she responded to your voice alone, and unresponsive would mean no response to pain at all.

lessons.title: Sick or not sick, and the transport decision
lessons.body:
## The only question that changes the next ten minutes

Experienced providers form one judgment fast: **sick or not sick.** It is not a diagnosis. It is a bet on whether this patient is compensating well or sliding, and it decides whether you stay and work or pick them up and go.

The body has a fixed set of moves when perfusion drops. It speeds up the heart, clamps down peripheral vessels, and increases breathing. That is why the sick signs are so consistent across very different diseases.

## Signs that mean sick

- **Skin:** pale, cool, and sweaty (diaphoretic), or mottled, or blue around the lips (cyanosis). Skin is the first organ the body sacrifices.
- **Mental status:** anything other than alert and oriented, or a patient who was alert and is now confused, agitated, or sleepy. Brain change means brain perfusion change until proven otherwise.
- **Breathing:** rate over 30 or under 8, tripod position, accessory muscles, retractions, one- to three-word sentences, or silence in someone who should be wheezing.
- **Circulation:** no radial pulse, a heart rate over 120 or under 50 with symptoms, capillary refill over 2 seconds.
- **Behavior:** the patient who says "I think I am going to die" is frequently right. Impending doom is a real finding.
- **Position:** a patient who will not lie flat, or who is too weak to sit up.

> **Key:** Blood pressure is a late sign. A healthy adult can lose 30 percent of blood volume with a normal systolic. Heart rate, skin, and mental status change first.

## Load-and-go versus stay-and-play

Some problems get fixed on scene. Some only get fixed in an operating room or a cath lab, and every minute on scene is a minute stolen from that.

**Load-and-go** is for patients whose problem is outside your scope: penetrating torso trauma, uncontrolled internal bleeding, an unstable airway you cannot manage, a suspected stroke inside the treatment window, a heart attack that needs a catheterization lab. Do the primary survey, fix what you can en route, and drive.

**Stay-and-play** is for patients whose problem you can actually treat where they are: a hypoglycemic diabetic who wakes up with oral glucose, an asthmatic who improves after an albuterol treatment, a patient who needs extrication before any movement is safe.

The benchmark taught nationally for critical trauma is a **scene time of 10 minutes or less**. That is not a rule you will always meet, and entrapment resets the clock, but if you are past 10 minutes with a critical patient you should be able to say exactly why.

## The ALS intercept

In New Jersey, BLS ambulances and ALS units are dispatched separately, so a paramedic arrives by a second vehicle rather than as part of your crew. If your patient needs ALS interventions such as cardiac monitoring, IV medications, or advanced airway management, you request the intercept early and you do not sit still waiting for it. You begin transport toward the hospital and meet the medics on the way.

> **On the exam:** If a question describes a critical patient and offers a choice between finishing an assessment on scene and transporting with assessment en route, the answer is transport.
keyPoints: Sick or not sick is a perfusion judgment, and it drives the transport decision.
Skin, mental status, and heart rate change before blood pressure does.
Load-and-go for problems you cannot fix; stay-and-play for problems you can.
Target scene time for critical trauma is 10 minutes or less.
Request an ALS intercept early and move toward the hospital rather than waiting in place.

checks.q: Which finding most strongly suggests a patient is 'sick' even though the blood pressure is still normal?
choices: A reported headache for two days
Cool, pale, sweaty skin with a heart rate of 124
A temperature of 37.6 C
A history of hypertension
checks.why: Cool pale diaphoretic skin plus tachycardia is the body compensating for poor perfusion. Blood pressure falls late, so a normal pressure does not reassure you here.

checks.q: A 34-year-old has a stab wound to the left chest, is anxious, and has a weak radial pulse. Best plan?
choices: Complete a full head-to-toe exam on scene, then transport
Transport immediately, performing further assessment en route
Wait on scene for the ALS unit to arrive
Have the patient walk to the ambulance to save time
checks.why: Penetrating torso trauma is a surgical problem, so this is load-and-go. Detailed exams and waiting in place both burn time the patient needs in an operating room.

lessons.title: History: the story the patient tells you
lessons.body:
## Most diagnoses live in the history

In emergency medicine, the story gets you closer to the answer than the exam does. Your job is to collect it in a structure you can hand off in 30 seconds.

Start with the **chief complaint**: the reason for the call, in the patient's own words, ideally short. "Chest pressure for two hours" is a chief complaint. "Rule out myocardial infarction" is not, because that is your idea, not theirs.

## Open first, then closed

Begin with an open question, which is a question that cannot be answered in one word: "What is going on today?" Then be quiet. People fill silence with useful information, and interrupting early is the single most common history-taking error.

Once you have the shape of the story, narrow with closed questions that pin down specifics: "Does the pain move anywhere?" "Have you taken your own nitroglycerin?" Ask one question at a time and wait for the answer.

## SAMPLE: the whole patient

- **S, signs and symptoms.** A sign is something you observe (pale skin, a deformity). A symptom is something only the patient can report (nausea, pain).
- **A, allergies.** Medications, foods, latex. "No known drug allergies" is charted as NKDA.
- **M, medications.** Prescriptions, over the counter, inhalers, herbals, and whether they have actually been taking them. Bring the bottles or photograph the list.
- **P, past medical history.** Prior heart attacks, diabetes, seizures, surgeries, and whether this feels like something that has happened before.
- **L, last oral intake.** What and when. It matters for hypoglycemia, for aspiration risk, and for the operating room.
- **E, events leading up.** What was the patient doing when it started, and what has changed since.

## OPQRST: the complaint in detail

Use this for pain, and for shortness of breath, dizziness, or nausea just as well.

- **O, onset.** Sudden or gradual, and doing what? A tearing pain that started at maximum intensity is different from an ache that built over a day.
- **P, provocation and palliation.** What makes it worse, what makes it better. Worse with a deep breath points at lung or chest wall; worse with exertion points at the heart.
- **Q, quality.** In their words: crushing, sharp, burning, tearing, pressure.
- **R, region and radiation.** Where it is, where it travels. Cardiac pain classically moves to the jaw, neck, or left arm.
- **S, severity.** A 0 to 10 scale, now and at its worst. The trend matters more than the number.
- **T, time.** How long, constant or intermittent, and is it getting better or worse.

## Pertinent negatives

A **pertinent negative** is a symptom you specifically asked about and the patient denies, when its absence changes the picture. Chest pain with no shortness of breath, no nausea, and no radiation is a different patient from one with all three. Documenting "denies shortness of breath" proves you asked, and proving you asked is half of what a good chart does.

> **Trap:** "Are you allergic to anything?" gets a no from a patient who forgets that penicillin gave her hives at age nine. Ask specifically about medication reactions and what the reaction was.

> **On the exam:** SAMPLE is the whole-patient history and OPQRST drills into the chief complaint. Questions that ask about the current pain want OPQRST; questions about background want SAMPLE.
keyPoints: Chief complaint is in the patient's words, not your suspected diagnosis.
Open question first, then silence, then closed questions one at a time.
SAMPLE covers the whole patient: signs/symptoms, allergies, meds, past history, last intake, events.
OPQRST drills into the complaint: onset, provocation, quality, radiation, severity, time.
Pertinent negatives are the symptoms you asked about and the patient denied, and they belong in the chart.

checks.q: Which question is an open question appropriate for starting a history?
choices: Does the pain go to your left arm?
Have you taken aspirin today?
Tell me what has been going on.
Is the pain sharp or dull?
checks.why: An open question cannot be answered in one word and lets the patient shape the story. The other three are closed questions, useful later to pin down specifics.

checks.q: A patient with abdominal pain says eating makes it worse. Which letter of OPQRST does that answer?
choices: O, onset
P, provocation and palliation
R, region and radiation
T, time
checks.why: Anything that makes the symptom better or worse is provocation and palliation. Onset is how it started, region is where it is, and time is duration and trend.

checks.q: Your chest pain patient specifically denies nausea and shortness of breath. How should this be handled?
choices: Leave it out, since only positive findings matter
Document it as a pertinent negative
Record it under allergies
Repeat the question until she reports a symptom
checks.why: Symptoms you asked about and the patient denied are pertinent negatives; they narrow the differential and document that you asked. Omitting them makes the chart look like the question was never posed.

lessons.title: Secondary assessment: head to toe, or focused
lessons.body:
## Two different exams for two different patients

The **secondary assessment** is the detailed physical exam you do after life threats are handled. Which version you run depends on what kind of patient you have.

**Rapid trauma assessment**, a fast head-to-toe, is for patients with a significant mechanism of injury or an altered mental status, because they cannot tell you where they hurt and the injury may be somewhere nobody is pointing. It takes 60 to 90 seconds.

**Focused exam** is for the responsive medical patient or the isolated injury. A patient with an ankle deformity from stepping off a curb does not need you palpating her skull. You examine the body system the complaint points at.

## What counts as a significant mechanism

Falls greater than 20 feet in an adult or greater than 10 feet (or three times the child's height) in a child. Ejection from a vehicle. Death of another occupant in the same vehicle. Rollover. Intrusion of more than 12 inches at the occupant site. Auto versus pedestrian. Motorcycle crash. Penetrating injury to head, neck, torso, or proximal limbs. Any of those buys a head-to-toe exam even if the patient feels fine.

## DCAP-BTLS

As your hands move over each region, you are looking and feeling for the same eight things:

- **D**eformities
- **C**ontusions (bruises)
- **A**brasions (scrapes)
- **P**unctures or penetrations
- **B**urns
- **T**enderness
- **L**acerations (cuts)
- **S**welling

The order of travel is head, neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, extremities, back. Specific additions per region:

- **Head:** feel the whole skull, check pupils, look for blood or clear fluid from ears or nose.
- **Neck:** midline tenderness, distended jugular veins (JVD), tracheal position, and any subcutaneous air that crackles under your fingers. Collar goes on here if indicated.
- **Chest:** look for symmetry and paradoxical motion, feel for crepitus, listen to lung sounds at four points minimum.
- **Abdomen:** press all four quadrants for rigidity, guarding, or tenderness. Press the painful quadrant last.
- **Pelvis:** press gently inward and downward once. If it is unstable or painful, stop pressing, because repeating it breaks clots.
- **Extremities:** all four, checking pulse, motor, and sensation distal to any injury before and after splinting.
- **Back:** log-roll the patient once and check it. The back is the single most skipped region and it is where posterior wounds hide.

> **Trap:** A patient with a distracting injury, alcohol on board, or a head injury does not feel a fractured pelvis. The lower the mental status, the more you rely on your hands and the less you rely on what they tell you.

> **On shift:** In the emergency department the trauma team does this same sweep as the secondary survey while a tech cuts clothing off, applies the monitor, and keeps the patient warm. Knowing the order means you are handing the physician the next item before it is asked for.
keyPoints: Rapid head-to-toe for significant mechanism or altered mental status; focused exam for responsive medical or isolated injury.
DCAP-BTLS is the checklist your hands run in every region.
Significant mechanisms include falls over 20 feet, ejection, rollover, death in the same vehicle, and penetrating torso trauma.
Press the painful abdominal quadrant last, and press an unstable pelvis only once.
Check pulse, motor, and sensation distal to an injury before and after splinting.

checks.q: Which patient should receive a rapid head-to-toe assessment rather than a focused exam?
choices: Alert adult with an isolated finger laceration from a kitchen knife
Alert adult with a sore throat and fever
Adult ejected from a rolled vehicle, now confused
Alert teenager with a twisted ankle from a curb
checks.why: Ejection is a significant mechanism and confusion means the patient cannot direct you to injuries, so the exam must cover everything. The other three are isolated or clearly medical complaints suited to a focused exam.

checks.q: What does the T in DCAP-BTLS stand for?
choices: Trauma
Tenderness
Tachycardia
Tension
checks.why: DCAP-BTLS is deformities, contusions, abrasions, punctures, burns, tenderness, lacerations, swelling. Tenderness is what the patient reports when you palpate, and it is often the only clue to a fracture you cannot see.

checks.q: You palpate a pelvis and feel it shift. What should you do next?
choices: Press again to confirm the finding
Stop palpating the pelvis and note the instability
Have the patient stand to test stability
Palpate more firmly on both sides
checks.why: An unstable pelvis is checked once. Repeat pressure disrupts clots and worsens bleeding into a space that can hold liters of blood, and standing the patient is never a stability test.

lessons.title: Vitals, trends, and reassessment
lessons.body:
## One set of vitals tells you almost nothing

A blood pressure of 118/72 is meaningless by itself. It matters because 20 minutes ago it was 148/88, or because it was 92/60 and is climbing. **Vital signs are only useful as a trend**, which is why you take a baseline set as early as possible and then keep repeating them.

## The baseline set

For an adult, the numbers you should know cold:

| Sign | Normal adult | Concerning |
|---|---|---|
| Heart rate | 60 to 100 | Under 50, over 120 |
| Respiratory rate | 12 to 20 | Under 8, over 30 |
| Systolic BP | 90 to 140 | Under 90 |
| Oxygen saturation | 94 to 99 percent | Under 94 percent |
| Capillary refill | Under 2 seconds | Over 2 seconds |
| Temperature | 36.5 to 37.5 C | Over 38 C, under 35 C |

Pulse: rate, strength (strong, weak, thready), and rhythm (regular or irregular). Radial for adults, brachial for infants.

Respirations: count for 30 seconds and double it, without telling the patient you are counting, because people who know they are being watched change how they breathe. Note effort and depth, not just rate.

Skin: color, temperature, moisture. In darker skin check the nail beds, the inside of the lip, and the conjunctiva for pallor or cyanosis.

Pupils: **PERRL**, pupils equal, round, reactive to light. Pinpoint pupils suggest opioids, blown or unequal pupils suggest a brain problem.

Pulse oximetry reads the percentage of hemoglobin carrying something. Target is generally `94%` or higher, except for a COPD patient where `88%` to `92%` may be the goal, and for carbon monoxide poisoning where a standard pulse oximeter reads falsely high and cannot be trusted at all.

Blood glucose: normal fasting is roughly `70` to `99 mg/dL`. Below `70 mg/dL` is hypoglycemia and is a reversible cause of altered mental status you must rule out in every confused patient.

## Reassessment intervals

After the primary survey, treatment, and the secondary assessment, you begin the **reassessment**, and you repeat it until you hand the patient over.

- **Unstable patient: every 5 minutes.**
- **Stable patient: every 15 minutes.**
- **Any time you give a treatment or the patient changes: immediately.**

Each reassessment repeats four things: mental status, the ABCs, vital signs, and the effect of every intervention you performed. You are asking two questions. Is the trend moving the right way, and did what I did work?

> **Key:** Unstable means every 5 minutes. If you are unsure whether a patient is stable, use the 5-minute interval, because the cost of extra vitals is nothing and the cost of missing a decline is everything.

> **On the exam:** A vignette that describes worsening numbers is telling you the patient is decompensating, even if each individual value is still in a normal range. A heart rate climbing 88 to 104 to 122 with a falling pulse pressure is shock in progress.
keyPoints: Vitals matter as a trend; the baseline set exists so later sets have meaning.
Unstable patients are reassessed every 5 minutes, stable patients every 15.
Reassessment repeats mental status, ABCs, vitals, and the effect of each intervention.
Target SpO2 is generally 94 percent or higher; pulse oximetry is unreliable in carbon monoxide poisoning.
Check a glucose on every altered patient; under 70 mg/dL is a reversible cause.

checks.q: Your patient is hypotensive and confused after a fall. How often do you reassess?
choices: Every 5 minutes
Every 15 minutes
Every 30 minutes
Once more before arrival
checks.why: Hypotension plus altered mental status makes this an unstable patient, and unstable patients get reassessed every 5 minutes so a decline is caught while you can still act.

checks.q: A patient rescued from a house fire has an SpO2 of 99 percent but is confused and has a headache. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Oxygenation is fine, look for another cause entirely
The pulse oximeter may read falsely high because of carbon monoxide
The reading confirms there is no inhalation injury
The patient is hyperventilating
checks.why: A standard pulse oximeter cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so it reads high in carbon monoxide poisoning. Treating the number instead of the patient in a fire victim is a classic and dangerous error.

checks.q: You take serial vitals: HR 88 then 104 then 122, BP 132/78 then 124/86 then 112/94. What is happening?
choices: The patient is improving
The patient is compensating for shock
The readings are within normal limits and need no action
The patient is likely febrile
checks.why: A rising heart rate with a narrowing pulse pressure is classic compensated shock. Each set is individually near normal, which is exactly why trends, not single values, drive the decision.

lessons.title: Medical flow versus trauma flow
lessons.body:
## Same skeleton, different order

Scene size-up and primary survey are identical for everyone. After that, the two paths diverge, and knowing which one you are on keeps you from wasting time.

## The medical patient

For a responsive medical patient, the **history is the exam**. You go from the primary survey straight to the chief complaint, OPQRST, and SAMPLE, then do a focused physical exam aimed at the system involved, then vitals, then treat.

Chest pain gets a look at skin, lung sounds, jugular veins, and leg swelling. Shortness of breath gets lung sounds, work of breathing, ability to speak in full sentences, and pulse oximetry. Abdominal pain gets all four quadrants and a last oral intake. You are not palpating the skull of a patient with a kidney stone.

For an **unresponsive** medical patient the order flips. You cannot get a history, so you perform a rapid head-to-toe first looking for clues, then collect the history from anyone and anything else available.

## The trauma patient

For trauma, **the mechanism drives the exam**. With a significant mechanism or an altered mental status, you do the rapid head-to-toe before anything focused, because the injury that kills may be somewhere the patient never mentions.

With a minor, isolated mechanism and an alert patient, you go focused. A cut finger from a kitchen knife is examined at the finger.

History in trauma is shorter and later. You still want SAMPLE, especially blood thinners in the medication list, but you get it while moving.

## Side by side

| Step | Responsive medical | Significant trauma |
|---|---|---|
| After primary survey | History (OPQRST, SAMPLE) | Rapid head-to-toe with DCAP-BTLS |
| Physical exam | Focused on the system | Full body, then focused |
| History timing | Early, drives everything | Later, often en route |
| Scene time | Often longer, treat on scene | 10 minutes or less if critical |
| Main question | What is wrong inside? | What did the forces break? |

> **Key:** Responsive medical patients get history then exam. Unresponsive medical and significant trauma patients get exam then history.

## When the two blur

Real calls mix. The elderly man found on the floor may have fallen because he had a stroke, or had a stroke because he fell. The driver who crashed may have crashed because of a seizure or low blood sugar. When the cause is unclear, run both: check a glucose and a mental status on your trauma patient, and look for injuries on your medical patient.

> **On shift:** "Found down" is the phrase that should make you run both paths. Ask how long they were down, because a patient on a hard floor for hours has pressure injury and muscle breakdown on top of whatever put them there.
keyPoints: Size-up and primary survey are identical for medical and trauma patients.
Responsive medical: history first, then a focused exam on the involved system.
Unresponsive medical and significant trauma: rapid head-to-toe exam first, history after.
Mechanism drives the trauma exam; the chief complaint drives the medical exam.
When the cause is unclear, run both paths, including a glucose check.

checks.q: A 55-year-old is alert with two hours of crushing chest pain. What comes next after the primary survey?
choices: Rapid head-to-toe with DCAP-BTLS
Focused history using OPQRST and SAMPLE
Log roll to check the back
Palpate the pelvis
checks.why: This is a responsive medical patient, so the history is where the answer lives and it comes before the exam. Head-to-toe trauma sweeps are for significant mechanism or altered patients.

checks.q: An unresponsive adult is found on a kitchen floor with no witnesses. Best approach?
choices: Wait for family before doing anything
Rapid head-to-toe exam plus glucose check, then gather history from any source
Focused exam of the abdomen only
Assume intoxication and transport without an exam
checks.why: With no history available you must let your hands and your meters do the work, and hypoglycemia is a reversible cause you can fix. Assuming intoxication is how strokes and head bleeds get missed.

lessons.title: Hard cases: altered, unresponsive, and refusing
lessons.body:
## The unresponsive medical patient: assume the worst

When nobody can tell you what happened, you assume the most dangerous explanation that fits and work backward. The memory aid is **AEIOU-TIPS**: Alcohol, Epilepsy, Insulin, Overdose, Uremia (kidney failure), Trauma, Infection, Psychiatric, Stroke or Shock.

Three things you can actually check in minutes:

1. **Glucose.** Under `70 mg/dL` is hypoglycemia. An awake patient who can swallow and protect their own airway gets oral glucose, typically `15 g` of gel.
2. **Pupils and breathing.** Pinpoint pupils with a respiratory rate under 12 is opioid overdose until proven otherwise. Where protocol allows EMTs to carry it, naloxone is `4 mg` intranasal, the whole single-dose device sprayed into one nostril, repeated in the other nostril as needed.
3. **Signs of stroke.** Facial droop, arm drift, slurred speech. Establish the last known well time, because it decides which treatments the hospital can offer.

Then become a detective. Search for medication bottles, a medical alert bracelet or necklace, an insulin pen, a dialysis shunt, an implanted port. Ask bystanders what the patient was doing in the last hour and whether this has happened before. Take the bottles with you.

> **Trap:** "Just drunk" and "just a psych patient" are the two most dangerous assessments in EMS. Both are diagnoses of exclusion, and both have killed patients with head bleeds, low sodium, and low blood sugar.

## Altered mental status in general

Altered mental status (AMS) is not a diagnosis, it is a finding, and it always earns a glucose check, a set of vitals, and a hard look for trauma. Compare against baseline: a family member saying "she is not herself" is a clinical finding, and in an elderly patient new confusion is frequently an infection, most often urinary or pulmonary.

## The patient who refuses

A refusal is the highest-risk call an EMT runs, because nobody is watching and the consequences appear later. To refuse, a patient must have **decision-making capacity**, which means all of the following:

- An adult, or an emancipated minor
- Alert and oriented, with a normal mental status for them
- Not impaired by alcohol, drugs, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, or head injury
- Able to explain back, in their own words, what is wrong, what could happen, and what they are giving up

A patient with a head injury, a low glucose, or a blood alcohol level that impairs judgment cannot legally refuse, and treatment proceeds under **implied consent**.

The sequence that protects both of you:

1. Assess fully. You cannot document a refusal on a patient you never examined.
2. Confirm capacity, and write down exactly how you confirmed it.
3. Explain the specific risks in plain words, including death or permanent harm where it is genuinely possible.
4. Offer alternatives: call again at any time, have someone stay with them, see their own doctor today.
5. Contact medical direction if the refusal is high risk, and document that you did.
6. Get the signature, plus a witness signature, ideally someone not on your crew.

> **On the exam:** The tested sequence is capacity, risks, alternatives, medical direction, signature with witness. Leaving out the risks conversation is the classic wrong answer.
keyPoints: AEIOU-TIPS covers the causes of unresponsiveness; glucose, pupils, and stroke signs are checkable in minutes.
Medication bottles, bracelets, ports, and shunts are history you can collect without the patient.
'Just drunk' and 'just psych' are diagnoses of exclusion and get people killed.
Capacity requires an unimpaired adult who can repeat back the risks in their own words.
Refusal sequence: full assessment, capacity, risks, alternatives, medical direction, signed and witnessed.

checks.q: An unresponsive adult has pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 6. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Stroke
Opioid overdose
Hypoglycemia
Heat stroke
checks.why: Pinpoint pupils plus respiratory depression is the opioid pattern. Hypoglycemia does not constrict pupils that way, and stroke findings are typically one-sided rather than a whole-body slowdown in breathing.

checks.q: A 40-year-old with a head laceration and a GCS of 14 after hitting his head wants to refuse transport. What is correct?
choices: He may refuse because he is an adult
He cannot legally refuse because his head injury impairs capacity
Have him sign and leave immediately
Refusal is valid if a family member agrees
checks.why: A head injury that alters mental status removes decision-making capacity, so treatment proceeds under implied consent. Adulthood alone does not establish capacity, and family cannot consent on behalf of a competent adult.

checks.q: Which element is most often missing from a legally weak refusal?
choices: The patient's signature
The date on the form
A documented conversation about specific risks, including death
The crew member names
checks.why: A signature without evidence the patient was told the specific consequences does not show informed refusal. The risks conversation, in the patient's own words repeated back, is the part that holds up later.

cards.front: What are the six components of the scene size-up?
cards.back: BSI/PPE, scene safety, mechanism of injury or nature of illness, number of patients, additional resources needed, and the spinal precautions decision.

cards.front: What does BSI stand for and when do you apply it?
cards.back: Body substance isolation. Gloves on every call; add eye protection and a mask when splashing or coughing is likely, and a gown for childbirth or heavy bleeding.

cards.front: At how many patients does a call become a multiple-casualty incident for a single crew?
cards.back: Three or more. One crew can manage one or two patients; beyond that you request additional units and begin triage.

cards.front: What is the difference between mechanism of injury and nature of illness?
cards.back: MOI is the forces that hit the body in a trauma call. NOI is the medical reason 911 was called. Size-up decides which one you have.

cards.front: The scene is not safe. What do you do?
cards.back: Do not enter. Stage at a safe distance, request police or fire, and wait until the scene is declared safe. You cannot help anyone as a second patient.

cards.front: Which findings push you toward spinal precautions?
cards.back: A loading mechanism plus midline neck or back pain, numbness or weakness, altered mental status, intoxication, or a distracting injury.

cards.front: What is the single job of the primary survey?
cards.back: Find and immediately treat life threats. It is a hunt, not an exam, and it takes 60 to 90 seconds.

cards.front: What do the letters of AVPU stand for?
cards.back: Alert, responds to Verbal stimulus, responds to Painful stimulus, Unresponsive. Anything below Alert is an airway risk.

cards.front: What does XABCDE stand for and why is X first?
cards.back: eXsanguinating hemorrhage, Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Expose. X is first because a limb can bleed out in about three minutes despite a perfect airway.

cards.front: Where do you place a tourniquet and what do you record?
cards.back: 2 to 3 inches above the wound, not over a joint, tightened until bleeding stops. Record the time of application on the tourniquet and the chart.

cards.front: Snoring versus gurgling respirations: what does each mean?
cards.back: Snoring is the tongue obstructing, fixed by head-tilt chin-lift or jaw thrust. Gurgling is fluid, fixed by suction for no more than 10 seconds at a time in an adult.

cards.front: At what adult respiratory rates do you assist ventilations, and at what rate?
cards.back: Slower than 8 or faster than 30 per minute with inadequate tidal volume. Bag-valve-mask at 1 breath every 6 seconds, which is 10 per minute.

cards.front: What systolic blood pressure does a palpable radial pulse suggest?
cards.back: Roughly 80 mmHg or higher. Losing the radial pulse while keeping a carotid suggests significant hypotension.

cards.front: What is a normal capillary refill time and what does a delay suggest?
cards.back: Under 2 seconds. Over 2 seconds suggests poor peripheral perfusion, though cold environments make it unreliable on their own.

cards.front: Why do you cover a trauma patient after exposing them?
cards.back: Hypothermia worsens clotting and bleeding. Cold, acidosis, and clotting failure form the trauma death spiral, and the blanket is a real intervention.

cards.front: Which vital sign changes last in shock, and why does that matter?
cards.back: Blood pressure. A healthy adult can lose about 30 percent of blood volume before the systolic drops, so heart rate, skin, and mental status warn you first.

cards.front: Name five findings that mark a patient as 'sick' on first impression.
cards.back: Pale cool sweaty or mottled skin, altered mental status, respiratory rate over 30 or under 8, absent radial pulse, and a patient who says they feel like they are dying.

cards.front: What is the target scene time for a critical trauma patient?
cards.back: 10 minutes or less. Entrapment resets the clock, but you should be able to state exactly why you exceeded it.

cards.front: Give three load-and-go conditions.
cards.back: Penetrating torso trauma, uncontrolled internal bleeding, an unstable airway you cannot manage, stroke in the treatment window, or a heart attack needing a cath lab.

cards.front: Give two stay-and-play situations.
cards.back: A hypoglycemic patient who wakes with oral glucose, an asthmatic who improves after albuterol, or a patient who must be extricated before any movement is safe.

cards.front: How do you handle an ALS intercept in a BLS system?
cards.back: Request it early and begin transport toward the hospital, meeting the paramedic unit en route. You do not sit on scene waiting for it.

cards.front: How should a chief complaint be recorded?
cards.back: In the patient's own words and as short as possible, such as chest pressure for two hours. Your suspected diagnosis is not the chief complaint.

cards.front: What does SAMPLE stand for?
cards.back: Signs and symptoms, Allergies, Medications, Past medical history, Last oral intake, Events leading up to the call.

cards.front: What does OPQRST stand for?
cards.back: Onset, Provocation and palliation, Quality, Region and radiation, Severity, Time. It drills into the chief complaint.

cards.front: What is the difference between a sign and a symptom?
cards.back: A sign is something you can observe or measure, such as pale skin or a pulse of 120. A symptom is something only the patient can report, such as nausea or pain.

cards.front: What is a pertinent negative and why document it?
cards.back: A symptom you specifically asked about that the patient denies, when its absence changes the picture. Documenting it narrows the differential and proves you asked.

cards.front: Why start a history with an open question and then stay quiet?
cards.back: Open questions let the patient shape the story and surface details you would not think to ask. Interrupting early is the most common history-taking error.

cards.front: Why does last oral intake matter?
cards.back: It informs hypoglycemia, aspiration risk during airway management, and the operating room's decision about anesthesia timing.

cards.front: Where does cardiac chest pain classically radiate?
cards.back: To the jaw, neck, shoulders, or left arm. Radiation is the R of OPQRST and it is a pattern worth asking about directly.

cards.front: What does DCAP-BTLS stand for?
cards.back: Deformities, Contusions, Abrasions, Punctures, Burns, Tenderness, Lacerations, Swelling. It is what your eyes and hands look for in every region.

cards.front: List four significant mechanisms of injury in an adult.
cards.back: Fall over 20 feet, ejection from a vehicle, death of another occupant, rollover, intrusion over 12 inches, auto versus pedestrian, motorcycle crash, penetrating torso injury.

cards.front: What is a significant fall height for a child?
cards.back: Greater than 10 feet, or more than three times the child's height. Adults use greater than 20 feet.

cards.front: In what order do you travel during a rapid head-to-toe exam?
cards.back: Head, neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, extremities, back. The back is the most frequently skipped region and hides posterior wounds.

cards.front: How many times do you palpate a pelvis and why?
cards.back: Once, gently inward and downward. If it is unstable or painful you stop, because repeat pressure disrupts clots in a space that can hold liters of blood.

cards.front: What do you check distal to any extremity injury?
cards.back: Pulse, motor function, and sensation, both before and after splinting. A change after splinting means the splint is too tight.

cards.front: Which abdominal quadrant do you palpate last?
cards.back: The one the patient says hurts. Pressing it first causes guarding that makes the rest of the exam unreliable.

cards.front: Give the normal adult ranges for heart rate, respiratory rate, and systolic blood pressure.
cards.back: Heart rate 60 to 100, respirations 12 to 20, systolic 90 to 140 mmHg.

cards.front: How often do you reassess an unstable patient versus a stable one?
cards.back: Unstable every 5 minutes, stable every 15 minutes, and immediately after any intervention or any change in the patient.

cards.front: What four things does every reassessment repeat?
cards.back: Mental status, the ABCs, vital signs, and the effect of every intervention you performed.

cards.front: What is the normal blood glucose range and the threshold for hypoglycemia?
cards.back: Roughly 70 to 99 mg/dL fasting. Below 70 mg/dL is hypoglycemia and is a reversible cause of altered mental status.

cards.front: What does PERRL stand for?
cards.back: Pupils Equal, Round, Reactive to Light. Pinpoint suggests opioids; unequal or nonreactive suggests a brain problem.

cards.front: When is a pulse oximeter reading untrustworthy?
cards.back: Carbon monoxide poisoning reads falsely high. It is also unreliable with poor perfusion, cold fingers, nail polish, or severe anemia.

cards.front: Why count respirations without telling the patient?
cards.back: People who know they are being watched change their breathing rate and depth. Count for 30 seconds and double it while appearing to hold the pulse.

cards.front: For a responsive medical patient, what follows the primary survey?
cards.back: The history: chief complaint, OPQRST, and SAMPLE, then a focused exam of the involved system, then vitals and treatment.

cards.front: For an unresponsive medical patient, what follows the primary survey?
cards.back: A rapid head-to-toe exam plus a glucose check, because no history is available. History comes afterward from bystanders, bottles, and bracelets.

cards.front: What decides whether a trauma patient gets a full head-to-toe or a focused exam?
cards.back: Mechanism and mental status. Significant mechanism or altered mental status means full head-to-toe; an isolated minor injury in an alert patient means focused.

cards.front: Why does 'found down' require running both the medical and trauma paths?
cards.back: The fall may have caused the problem or the problem may have caused the fall. Check glucose and mental status, and also examine for injuries and down time.

cards.front: What does AEIOU-TIPS stand for?
cards.back: Alcohol, Epilepsy, Insulin, Overdose, Uremia, Trauma, Infection, Psychiatric, Stroke or Shock. It is the differential for unresponsiveness.

cards.front: What three fast checks do you run on every unresponsive patient?
cards.back: Blood glucose, pupils with respiratory rate for opioid patterns, and stroke signs with a last known well time.

cards.front: What physical clues serve as history in a patient who cannot talk?
cards.back: Medication bottles, a medical alert bracelet or necklace, insulin pens, a dialysis shunt, an implanted port, and what bystanders saw in the last hour.

cards.front: What four conditions must be met for a patient to have decision-making capacity?
cards.back: Adult or emancipated minor, alert and oriented at their baseline, unimpaired by drugs, alcohol, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, or head injury, and able to repeat the risks back.

cards.front: What is the six-step refusal sequence?
cards.back: Full assessment, confirm and document capacity, explain specific risks, offer alternatives, contact medical direction if high risk, obtain signed and witnessed refusal.

cards.front: Why are 'just drunk' and 'just a psych patient' dangerous assessments?
cards.back: Both are diagnoses of exclusion. Head bleeds, low sodium, hypoglycemia, and hypoxia all look like intoxication or agitation, and all are missed by assuming.

quiz.q: You are dispatched to a residence for an 'unknown medical.' As you pull up, two people are fighting on the front lawn. What is your first action?
choices: Stage at a safe distance and request police
Approach and attempt to separate them
Enter the home through a side door to reach the patient
Begin triage of both people fighting
quiz.why: Scene safety precedes all patient care, and violence in progress means you stage and wait for law enforcement. Entering by another door does not make an active violent scene safe, and intervening physically is outside your role and makes you a patient.

quiz.q: Which item on the NREMT patient assessment skill sheet is NOT part of the scene size-up?
choices: Determines the number of patients
Considers the need for additional resources
Obtains a SAMPLE history
Determines the mechanism of injury or nature of illness
quiz.why: SAMPLE belongs to the history-taking portion, which happens after the primary survey. Number of patients, additional resources, and MOI/NOI are all scored inside the size-up, along with BSI, scene safety, and the spinal decision.

quiz.q: A 24-year-old is pinned under a car with an arterial bleed spraying from his upper arm and snoring respirations. What is your very first intervention?
choices: Jaw-thrust to open the airway
Apply high-flow oxygen by nonrebreather
Request fire for extrication
Apply a tourniquet to the upper arm
quiz.why: Massive external hemorrhage is the X that precedes A in XABCDE, because arterial bleeding can kill in about three minutes while a partially obstructed airway still moves air. The airway is next, and extrication is already needed but does not stop the bleeding.

quiz.q: An adult is breathing at 6 per minute with shallow chest rise after an overdose. What is the correct ventilation rate with a bag-valve mask?
choices: 1 breath every 3 seconds
1 breath every 6 seconds
1 breath every 10 seconds
1 breath every 15 seconds
quiz.why: Adults in respiratory failure with a pulse are ventilated at 1 breath every 6 seconds, or 10 per minute. Faster rates cause gastric distension and drop venous return; slower rates fail to correct the carbon dioxide.

quiz.q: During the primary survey of a trauma patient, you find a radial pulse absent but a carotid pulse present. What does this suggest?
choices: Normal perfusion for a young adult
A systolic pressure likely below 80 mmHg
An arrhythmia unrelated to blood loss
An error in technique requiring no further action
quiz.why: Losing the radial while keeping the carotid means peripheral perfusion has failed, which corresponds to a systolic roughly under 80 mmHg. This is a decompensation finding, not a normal variant or a technique issue to shrug off.

quiz.q: Which set of findings best fits a patient who is 'sick' despite a normal blood pressure?
choices: Warm dry skin, HR 78, alert and oriented
Flushed skin, HR 92, complaining of a headache
Warm skin, HR 66, reports two days of cough
Cool pale diaphoretic skin, HR 126, mildly confused
quiz.why: Tachycardia with cool pale sweaty skin and a mental status change is compensated shock, and blood pressure is the last thing to fall. The other options describe intact perfusion, where normal skin and mental status are reassuring.

quiz.q: A critical trauma patient is packaged and ready, but the ALS unit is 12 minutes out and the hospital is 9 minutes away. Best decision?
choices: Begin transport and request an ALS intercept en route
Wait on scene for ALS to arrive
Cancel ALS and transport without notifying the hospital
Complete a detailed secondary assessment before moving
quiz.why: Transport time is shorter than the ALS response, so moving toward definitive care while requesting an intercept gives the patient both. Waiting wastes minutes, canceling notification removes the trauma team's head start, and detailed exams belong en route.

quiz.q: Which of the following is the best example of a properly recorded chief complaint?
choices: Possible myocardial infarction
Chest pressure for two hours
Patient appears unwell
Hypertension and diabetes
quiz.why: The chief complaint is the patient's reason for calling, in their words and time-anchored. A suspected diagnosis is your interpretation, a general impression is not a complaint, and a list of chronic conditions is past medical history.

quiz.q: A patient with abdominal pain says the pain started suddenly while she was sitting still. Which OPQRST element does this answer?
choices: Onset
Quality
Severity
Time
quiz.why: Onset covers how the symptom began and what the patient was doing. Quality is the character of the pain, severity is the 0 to 10 rating, and time is how long it has lasted and whether it is constant.

quiz.q: You ask a shortness-of-breath patient an open question and she begins a long answer. What is the most appropriate response?
choices: Interrupt with a closed question to save time
Ask the family to answer instead
Move immediately to vital signs
Let her finish, then narrow with closed questions
quiz.why: Patients surface details you would not think to ask for, and interrupting early is the most common history error. Closed questions are the right follow-up, but they come after the story, not instead of it.

quiz.q: Which is a pertinent negative in a patient complaining of crushing chest pain?
choices: Denies shortness of breath and nausea
Has a history of hypertension
Takes metoprolol daily
Ate lunch two hours ago
quiz.why: A pertinent negative is a symptom you asked about that the patient denies, and its absence changes the clinical picture. Hypertension is past history, metoprolol is a medication, and lunch is last oral intake.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old fell 25 feet from scaffolding and is alert but only complains of ankle pain. What exam is indicated?
choices: Rapid head-to-toe assessment
Focused exam of the ankle only
No physical exam, transport only
Abdominal exam only
quiz.why: A fall greater than 20 feet is a significant mechanism, and adrenaline plus a distracting injury routinely hides other trauma. Examining only the ankle is how a spinal or abdominal injury leaves the scene undetected.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT included in DCAP-BTLS?
choices: Contusions
Punctures
Crepitus
Swelling
quiz.why: DCAP-BTLS is deformities, contusions, abrasions, punctures, burns, tenderness, lacerations, swelling. Crepitus is a real and important finding when you palpate a chest, but it is not one of the eight letters.

quiz.q: While assessing a motorcycle crash victim, your partner skips the log roll because the patient denies back pain. What is the risk?
choices: None, since the patient can report pain reliably
Missing posterior wounds or spinal deformity
Prolonged scene time with no benefit
Increased risk of hypothermia only
quiz.why: The back is where posterior penetrating wounds and step-offs hide, and pain reporting is unreliable with adrenaline, distracting injuries, or intoxication. One controlled log roll is fast and is the only way to see that surface.

quiz.q: Which finding on a rapid trauma assessment of the neck most urgently suggests a chest problem?
choices: A small abrasion over the clavicle
Tenderness of the posterior neck muscles
A healed surgical scar
Distended jugular veins with tracheal deviation
quiz.why: Jugular venous distension with tracheal deviation points toward tension pneumothorax, a life threat that demands immediate action. Abrasions and old scars are incidental, and muscular tenderness alone is not a chest emergency.

quiz.q: Your patient is stable with an isolated forearm fracture on a 20-minute transport. How often should you reassess?
choices: Every 5 minutes
Every 15 minutes
Every 30 minutes
Only on arrival
quiz.why: Stable patients are reassessed every 15 minutes, and after splinting you would also recheck pulse, motor, and sensation immediately. The 5-minute interval is reserved for unstable patients or anyone you are unsure about.

quiz.q: You give albuterol to a wheezing patient. When do you reassess?
choices: Immediately after the treatment
At the 15-minute mark on schedule
Only if the patient reports a change
On arrival at the emergency department
quiz.why: Every intervention is followed by an immediate reassessment to see whether it worked, independent of the scheduled interval. Waiting for the patient to volunteer a change delays recognizing that the treatment failed.

quiz.q: Serial vitals on a 22-year-old after a motorcycle crash: HR 92 to 110 to 128, BP 128/70 to 118/80 to 108/92, skin cool. Interpretation?
choices: Anxiety from the crash
A normal response to pain that needs no action
Progressive compensated shock from internal bleeding
Improving perfusion
quiz.why: A rising heart rate with a narrowing pulse pressure and cool skin is the body clamping down on a falling blood volume. Anxiety does not narrow pulse pressure or cool the skin, and nothing in the trend is improving.

quiz.q: A COPD patient has an SpO2 of 90 percent, speaks in full sentences, and is alert. What is the most appropriate action?
choices: Immediately begin bag-valve-mask ventilation
Withhold oxygen entirely
Apply a nonrebreather at 15 L/min regardless of response
Titrate oxygen toward a target of about 88 to 92 percent and monitor
quiz.why: Chronic COPD patients are often targeted to 88 to 92 percent, and this patient is speaking in full sentences and alert, which means ventilation is adequate. Bagging an adequately breathing patient and blindly maximizing oxygen are both overtreatment.

quiz.q: Which sequence is correct for an alert 60-year-old with sudden shortness of breath?
choices: Primary survey, history, focused exam, vitals
Primary survey, rapid head-to-toe, history, vitals
History, primary survey, vitals, focused exam
Vitals, history, primary survey, focused exam
quiz.why: A responsive medical patient gets the history immediately after the primary survey, because the story points at the system to examine. Head-to-toe sweeps belong to trauma or altered patients, and the primary survey always comes before history and vitals.

quiz.q: An 80-year-old is found on the bathroom floor, confused, with a bruised forehead. What is the best approach?
choices: Treat as trauma only and immobilize
Treat as medical only and check glucose
Run both paths: glucose and neuro check plus a head-to-toe trauma exam
Defer assessment until family arrives with history
quiz.why: The fall may have caused the confusion or the confusion may have caused the fall, so committing to one path guarantees a miss. Deferring the assessment wastes the window for stroke and hypoglycemia recognition.

quiz.q: An unresponsive 46-year-old has a respiratory rate of 6 and pinpoint pupils. Which is the most appropriate next step after airway management?
choices: Administer oral glucose
Apply a cervical collar and transport
Assist ventilations and consider naloxone per protocol
Perform a detailed head-to-toe exam before any treatment
quiz.why: Respiratory depression with pinpoint pupils is an opioid pattern, and ventilation is what keeps the patient alive while naloxone is prepared. Oral glucose in an unresponsive patient risks aspiration, and detailed exams never precede treating hypoventilation.

quiz.q: Which of these patients may legally refuse transport?
choices: A 17-year-old with a wrist injury whose parents are unreachable
A 45-year-old with a blood glucose of 42 mg/dL
A 38-year-old, alert and oriented times four, sober, who repeats the risks back to you
A 52-year-old with a head injury who cannot recall the crash
quiz.why: Capacity requires an unimpaired adult who understands and can restate the consequences. A minor without a guardian, a hypoglycemic patient, and a head-injured patient with amnesia all lack capacity, and care proceeds under implied consent.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of steps when a competent adult refuses care after a significant mechanism?
choices: Get a signature, then explain the risks
Leave immediately and document later from memory
Have a family member sign on the patient's behalf
Assess, confirm capacity, explain risks, offer alternatives, contact medical direction, obtain signed and witnessed refusal
quiz.why: The protective sequence runs assessment, capacity, risks, alternatives, medical direction, signature with witness. Signing before the risks are explained is not informed refusal, and family cannot sign away a competent adult's decision.

quiz.q: A 28-year-old smells of alcohol, is agitated, and has a small scalp laceration after a fall. Which assumption is most dangerous?
choices: That he is simply intoxicated
That he may have a head injury
That his glucose could be low
That he may be hypoxic
quiz.why: Intoxication is a diagnosis of exclusion, and head bleeds, hypoglycemia, and hypoxia all produce agitation in someone who also happens to have been drinking. The other three assumptions all drive you toward assessments that protect the patient.

quiz.q: During a reassessment your patient's mental status drops from alert to responsive to verbal only. What is your priority?
choices: Continue the secondary assessment as planned
Document the change and recheck in 15 minutes
Recheck airway and breathing and upgrade the transport priority
Ask the patient to rate her pain again
quiz.why: A falling mental status threatens the airway and signals worsening perfusion or oxygenation, so you return to the ABCs and escalate. Continuing a detailed exam or waiting 15 minutes ignores the most sensitive deterioration sign you have.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: 58-year-old female, difficulty breathing
scenarios.intro: You are dispatched to a single-family home at 1420 for a 58-year-old female with difficulty breathing. Dispatch reports she is conscious and breathing. Your partner is driving; you are attending. Run this exactly the way the NREMT patient assessment medical station is graded: size-up, primary survey, history, secondary, vitals, reassessment.

steps.prompt:
You pull up to a quiet street. No traffic hazards, no crowd. The front door is open and a man waves you in.

What do you do before entering?

choices.text: State BSI and PPE, confirm the scene is safe, determine this is a medical call (nature of illness), and ask how many patients there are
choices.feedback: Correct. Six size-up points get graded separately: BSI, scene safety, MOI/NOI, number of patients, additional resources, and the spinal decision. Verbalize them.

choices.text: Walk in with the stretcher and find the patient first, then think about gloves
choices.feedback: Automatic failure criterion territory. The skill sheet fails a candidate who does not take or verbalize body substance isolation precautions before patient contact.

choices.text: Put on gloves and go in, deciding you will sort out the rest at the patient's side
choices.feedback: Gloves alone earn one point out of six. Scene safety, nature of illness, number of patients, and additional resources are separate scored items you just skipped.

steps.prompt:
The patient is sitting upright at the edge of the couch, leaning forward on her hands. Lips are dusky. She speaks in three-word bursts: "Can't... catch... breath." Audible wheezing without a stethoscope. Skin is warm and damp.

What is the primary survey here?

choices.text: General impression, AVPU, then airway, breathing with oxygen applied now, circulation, and a priority decision
choices.feedback: Right. She is alert but in respiratory distress with an SpO2 of 87 percent. Breathing is the life threat and you fix it inside the primary survey, not after it.

choices.text: Lay her flat to assess her airway properly
choices.feedback: Harmful. A patient in respiratory distress has chosen the position that works. Forcing a tripoding patient supine reduces tidal volume and can precipitate arrest.

choices.text: Move to history taking first since she is alert and can talk
choices.feedback: She cannot talk, she is producing three words at a time. Hypoxia at 87 percent is a life threat found in the primary survey and treated there.

choices.text: Apply oxygen, note the tripod position and dusky lips, and identify her as a high transport priority
choices.feedback: Good instinct and the treatment is right, but say the rest out loud: general impression, AVPU, and a circulation check are scored items on the sheet.

steps.prompt:
Oxygen is on. She is slightly easier to hear now. Her husband is standing next to you and answers questions readily.

How do you build the history?

choices.text: OPQRST on the breathing plus a full SAMPLE, using the husband to fill gaps she cannot
choices.feedback: Correct. OPQRST works for shortness of breath as well as pain. When the patient cannot speak in sentences, a reliable family member is a legitimate source and you document who told you.

choices.text: Ask only whether she has an inhaler, then move on
choices.feedback: You will get the inhaler point and lose everything else. Onset, what she was doing, prior episodes, allergies, and whether this feels like her usual asthma or something new all change the picture.

choices.text: Skip history entirely because she is a high priority and load her
choices.feedback: Skipping the history is a scored omission and clinically expensive. A first-ever episode at 58 with leg swelling is a very different patient from a known asthmatic having her usual flare.

steps.prompt:
History: onset one hour ago, gradual, worse lying down. She has had two similar episodes in the last week, each at night. Denies chest pain, denies fever, denies cough with sputum. Medications include lisinopril and furosemide. Past history of high blood pressure. She last ate dinner at 1830. She slept in a recliner last night because she could not lie flat.

What focused exam do you do?

choices.text: Full head-to-toe with DCAP-BTLS
choices.feedback: Wrong exam for this patient. DCAP-BTLS sweeps are for significant mechanism or altered patients. On a responsive medical patient you examine the system the history points at.

choices.text: Lung sounds in at least four fields, neck for jugular distension, ankles for swelling, and work of breathing
choices.feedback: Exactly the focused exam this history demands. Orthopnea, furosemide, and nighttime episodes point at heart failure, and jugular distension with crackles and leg edema would confirm the pattern.

choices.text: Palpate the abdomen in all four quadrants and check the pelvis
choices.feedback: Nothing in this history points at the abdomen or pelvis. A focused exam that ignores the chest in a breathing complaint misses the finding that decides treatment.

steps.prompt:
Exam: crackles in both bases, jugular veins distended at 45 degrees, ankles pitting to mid-shin. She is now moving air better on oxygen and speaking in short sentences.

You obtain a full baseline set of vitals. What else belongs in the baseline?

choices.text: Pulse quality and rhythm, skin color, temperature and moisture, pupils, and a blood glucose
choices.feedback: Correct. The skill sheet wants a complete set, and glucose is cheap insurance on any patient who could become altered. Her pressure of 186/104 with crackles fits acute heart failure.

choices.text: Just the pulse oximetry reading, since breathing is the problem
choices.feedback: Incomplete. A pulse oximeter number without a pulse quality, skin assessment, and blood pressure gives the receiving team almost nothing to trend against.

choices.text: Skip vitals and transport now, taking them at the hospital
choices.feedback: A baseline set is a scored item and the entire point of vitals is comparison over time. Without a baseline, nobody can tell whether your treatment helped.

steps.prompt:
She is in the ambulance, upright, on oxygen, and an ALS intercept is meeting you in four minutes. Transport time to the hospital is 14 minutes.

How do you manage the rest of the call?

choices.text: Reassess every 5 minutes: mental status, ABCs, vitals, and the effect of the oxygen, and give the medic a focused report at the intercept
choices.feedback: Correct. She is unstable, so the interval is 5 minutes, and each reassessment must include whether your intervention changed anything.

choices.text: Reassess every 15 minutes because she looks better on oxygen
choices.feedback: Looking better is not stable. Hypoxia, tachycardia, and acute heart failure make her unstable, and the 15-minute interval would give you exactly one reassessment for the whole trip.

choices.text: Lay her flat now that oxygen is on so she is easier to monitor
choices.feedback: Harmful. Flat is the position that triggered this episode in the first place. Upright reduces preload and is part of the treatment.

choices.text: Stop assessing and focus on writing the chart before arrival
choices.feedback: The chart waits. Reassessment is the only thing that detects deterioration, and an unstable patient left unwatched for 14 minutes is how arrests happen in the back of an ambulance.

scenarios.debrief: This is the medical flow: size-up, primary survey with the life threat treated on the spot, history before exam, a focused exam on the system the history named, a complete baseline, then 5-minute reassessments. The history did the diagnostic work here. Orthopnea, nighttime episodes, furosemide on the medication list, and a week of recurring night-time episodes pointed at heart failure before you ever touched her chest, and the exam simply confirmed it. On the NREMT medical assessment station, the critical failures that most often end a run are not verbalizing BSI, failing to treat a life threat when it is found, and failing to obtain a baseline set of vitals.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: motorcycle versus guardrail, one patient
scenarios.intro: You are dispatched at 2140 to a two-lane road for a motorcycle crash. Police are on scene. Dispatch reports one rider, down, conscious. It is dark and the road is open to traffic in the opposite lane. Run this as the NREMT trauma assessment station is graded.

steps.prompt:
You arrive to find a police car blocking one lane, traffic moving past in the other, a motorcycle on its side about 30 feet from the rider, and a helmet still on the patient.

What is your size-up?

choices.text: BSI and eye protection, confirm traffic control with police, identify a significant mechanism, confirm one patient, decide on resources, and call for spinal precautions
choices.feedback: Correct, all six points. A motorcycle crash with 30 feet of separation between rider and bike is a significant mechanism on its own, and the traffic lane still moving is an ongoing hazard you address before kneeling.

choices.text: Run directly to the patient because he is conscious and time matters
choices.feedback: A provider struck in a live traffic lane at night is the reason this fails. Scene safety and BSI are graded first, and both are quick.

choices.text: Put on gloves, note the crash, and approach
choices.feedback: Partial credit at best. You skipped eye protection at a bloody nighttime trauma scene, skipped confirming traffic control, and never stated the mechanism, patient count, resources, or spinal decision.

steps.prompt:
The rider is supine, moving his arms, moaning. His left thigh is grossly deformed and there is a large pool of blood under it soaking into the pavement. Breathing is fast and shallow. Helmet is on.

What is your primary survey?

choices.text: Manual in-line stabilization, then control the thigh bleeding immediately, then airway, breathing, circulation, disability, expose
choices.feedback: Correct. X comes before A. A growing pool from a deformed femur is life-threatening hemorrhage, and a tourniquet high on the thigh takes seconds while a partner holds the head.

choices.text: Remove the helmet first so you can see his face
choices.feedback: Wrong priority and a two-person maneuver done at the wrong moment. He is moaning, so he has an airway, and he is bleeding out from a leg while you work on his head.

choices.text: Start a head-to-toe exam to find all his injuries
choices.feedback: Detailed exams belong after life threats. On the trauma station, failing to manage the problems associated with airway, breathing, hemorrhage, or shock is a listed critical failure.

choices.text: Hold the head, apply high-flow oxygen, and control the thigh bleeding
choices.feedback: The interventions are right and in a defensible order. Say the rest out loud so it is scored: AVPU, breathing assessment, circulation check, disability, and expose.

steps.prompt:
Tourniquet is on at 2146 and the bleeding has stopped. Head is held. He opens his eyes to your voice, says his name, does not know what day it is, and repeats the same question three times.

What does this tell you and what do you do next?

choices.text: He is alert but disoriented, which means significant mechanism plus altered mental status, so he gets a rapid head-to-toe assessment
choices.feedback: Correct. Repeating questions is a head injury sign, and an altered patient cannot direct you to injuries. Full head-to-toe, not focused.

choices.text: He is talking, so run a focused exam on the deformed leg only
choices.feedback: Talking is not intact. He does not know the day and is perseverating, so his report of what hurts is unreliable and the leg is only the injury you can see.

choices.text: Assume he is intoxicated and defer further assessment
choices.feedback: Intoxication is a diagnosis of exclusion and never an assessment shortcut. This presentation after a motorcycle crash is a head injury until a scanner says otherwise.

steps.prompt:
Rapid head-to-toe: skull intact under a properly removed helmet, pupils equal, no fluid from ears, trachea midline, chest with symmetric rise and tenderness over the left lower ribs, abdomen soft, pelvis stable, left femur deformed, distal pulses present in all four limbs, back checked on the log roll with no wounds.

What did you use to structure that exam and what still needs doing?

choices.text: DCAP-BTLS in every region, and you still need a cervical collar, the femur splinted or the patient fully immobilized, and warmth
choices.feedback: Correct. The collar goes on at the neck check, the femur gets traction or immobilization per protocol, and a blanket is a real intervention because cold worsens bleeding.

choices.text: DCAP-BTLS, and nothing further is needed before transport
choices.feedback: The exam structure is right but the interventions are missing. Leaving a suspected spinal injury uncollared and a femur unsplinted are both scored omissions.

choices.text: You used OPQRST, and you now need a detailed pain history
choices.feedback: OPQRST drills a complaint; DCAP-BTLS structures a trauma exam. A confused patient with a femur fracture is not going to give you a reliable pain history, and it is not what he needs now.

steps.prompt:
He is collared, immobilized, splinted, covered with two blankets, on oxygen, and loaded. Scene time so far is 9 minutes. Trauma center is 16 minutes away; the nearest community hospital is 5 minutes away.

What is the plan?

choices.text: Transport to the trauma center, request an ALS intercept, notify the receiving facility, and reassess every 5 minutes
choices.feedback: Correct. A femur fracture with a tourniquet, a narrowing pulse pressure, and a GCS of 13 is a trauma center patient, and the extra 11 minutes buys a surgical team.

choices.text: Go to the closest hospital because he is unstable
choices.feedback: Defensible only if you cannot manage the airway or control bleeding. Here, bleeding is controlled and the airway is intact, and a community hospital will re-package him and re-transport, costing far more than 11 minutes.

choices.text: Stay on scene until vitals stabilize
choices.feedback: Nothing you carry will stabilize these vitals. Compensated hemorrhagic shock stabilizes in an operating room, and every minute on scene past the 10-minute benchmark works against him.

steps.prompt:
Eight minutes into transport he is quieter, harder to rouse, and his skin is cool and mottled at the knees.

What do you do?

choices.text: Reassess ABCs now, re-check the tourniquet for renewed bleeding, keep him warm, support ventilations if the rate or volume fails, and update the receiving trauma team
choices.feedback: Correct. Decompensation means you go back to the primary survey, not forward to the chart. A loosened tourniquet is a real and fixable cause of this trend.

choices.text: Let him rest since he has been agitated
choices.feedback: Harmful. A falling mental status in a bleeding trauma patient is decompensation, not rest, and it is the last warning you get before the airway goes.

choices.text: Wait for the scheduled 5-minute reassessment before acting
choices.feedback: Any change in the patient triggers an immediate reassessment regardless of the clock. The interval is a floor, not a ceiling.

choices.text: Remove the tourniquet to restore circulation to the leg
choices.feedback: Dangerous. Field tourniquets are not released by EMS in a patient who is decompensating; that decision belongs in a resuscitation bay with blood products ready.

scenarios.debrief: The trauma flow differs from the medical flow in one key way: the mechanism, not the history, decides the exam. Significant mechanism or altered mental status buys a full head-to-toe with DCAP-BTLS before any focused work, and the history comes later and shorter. Three things ran this call. X before A, because the femur was killing him faster than anything else. A scene time under 10 minutes, because his problem lives in an operating room. And reassessment every 5 minutes, which is what caught the decompensation at minute eight. On the NREMT trauma assessment station, the listed critical failures include not taking BSI precautions, failing to manage hemorrhage or shock, performing a detailed exam before addressing life threats, not providing spinal protection when indicated, and not transporting within the 10-minute window without a stated reason.
